content: Prices recalibrate higher as marginal costs increase; raising short-term prices and long-term price

Key takeaways from our iron ore market review: 1) China steel production was down 4.1% YTD in April – this is a relatively soft start to the year, but the April annualised rate is near 1bn tonnes, which is better than any month through 2H25 – steel exports were soft in Jan/Feb but recovered to 101/110Mtpa in March/April. 2) China’s YTD iron ore imports are up almost 30Mt – most of this has gone to port stocks, which are now showing signs of a drawdown after hitting record levels (likely BHP drawdown post CMRG negotiation outcome), and 3) Iron ore prices have risen since the beginning of the Middle East conflict despite better seaborne iron ore supply, and uninspiring China steel output. We attribute the price move to higher costs. Marginal miners have seen +7/t spot FOB cost inflation as a result of diesel/explosives price moves. Meanwhile, freight has also risen $5/t from WA, and $13/t from Brazil. We have updated our near-term prices by ~$5/t ($105/t / $99/t in 2026/27) to account for the higher cost curve. We have also raised our long-term real price from $80/t to $90/t (last updated in 2Q23) to reflect general inflation across inputs, reduced quality specifications (higher cost per Fe unit) and higher China steel run rate than previously forecast going into Simandou’s ramp-up (more marginal production remains in the market).

- China steel output down, exports bounce back, while iron ore imports rise YTD. China iron ore imports have been strong, up almost 30Mt YTD through April (+8%), with all major regions trending higher. Most of the increase in imports has gone to port stocks which reached 165Mt (record levels), but have since fallen ~5Mt. Non-traditional suppliers are the main driver of the port stock build. China's steel production was down 4.1% YTD through April, but the run rate is healthy, annualising ~1Btpa on NBS data, and above any month from Apr-Dec 2025. Interestingly, China steel exports printed 110Mtpa in April, recovering from Jan/Feb lows of ~90Mtpa. World ex China steel production is largely flat YTD, with global output down 2.2% through April.

- Iron ore mining costs are up – the cost curve has risen, but also steepened. The 2026 CFR cost curve has moved higher following the Middle East conflict, with associated increases in diesel, explosives, freight rates and other inputs. It’s also worth noting that since FY26 cost guidance was set, there have been unfavourable movements in the AUD & BRL (translates local costs into higher USD costs). We estimate FOB costs are up $1.1-7.4/t for the Australian miners, with CFR costs up $6-12/t. Interestingly, with iron ore up ~$6/t since the beginning of the ME conflict, Tier 1 producers in Australia have minimal impact from a margin perspective.

- CFR vs FOB prices post ME conflict – significant Brazil vs Australia variance: CFR quoted iron ore prices at ~$106/t include bulk freight rates that are up ~50% since the start of the conflict (link); Australia to China is currently $15/t (+5$/t), Brazil to China is $37/t (+$14/t). Consequently, FOB realised prices for Australian iron ore are +1% since ME conflict, but Brazil FOB prices are -10%. Higher freight has impacted Australian iron ore miners (BHP/RIO/FMG) much less than those in Brazil (Vale and Anglo American) and Africa iron ore miners (Kumba) where shipping distances to China are longer.
See page 51 for analyst certification and important disclosures, including non-US analyst disclosures.

- Raising our LT real price to $90/t. Many miners have recently reduced product quality, leading to higher cost/Fe unit (albeit in some cases this is associated with lower strip ratios). In addition, general inflation pressures (raw materials/labour/capex) have been very evident in mining. These factors have driven marginal iron ore costs higher, which, in our view, justifies raising long-term real prices from $80/t to $90/t, +12.5% (we last updated 2Q23). Finally, given the persistent run rates in China steel output around 1Bntpa, Simandou is likely to be less damaging to pricing dynamics than we previously expected (more marginal tonnes remain in the market). Our LT price upgrade is largely unrelated to the current cost pressures associated with the Middle East conflict.

- Iron ore price recalibrates higher with marginal costs: Iron ore has risen around $6/t since the beginning of the ME conflict with spot now at $106/t. In our view, this is more a reflection of higher marginal costs, than a demand driven bounce. We raise our 2026 / 2027 estimates $5/t to $105/99/t. Key risks continue to include the pace of Simandou's ramp-up, along with any potential global growth / steel demand impacts from the Middle East conflict.
Our 2026/27 price forecasts have risen, largely to reflect higher freight rates along with increased marginal costs related to diesel and other input price increases.

There has been significant pressure on marginal iron ore costs in recent years. This likely explains iron ore's resilience over $100/t, with any dip below $90/t met with supply curtailments (eg India has been very elastic). We now see the need for a higher long-term real price of $90/t vs our previous $80/t, +12.5% (we last updated in 2023). Our LT price upgrade is largely unrelated to the current cost pressures associated with the Middle East conflict. Key drivers are as follows:

- Reduced product quality: Recently, many iron ore miners have reduced product quality, which is essentially producing the same tonnage but with a lower Fe content. This has essentially increased the cost per Fe unit (some miners will benefit from lower strip ratios associated with this move, while for other miners it's just a function of ore body sequencing).

- Opex & capex inflation: Inflation pressures (raw materials/labour) have been very evident across global mining opex. Recent capex blowouts (e.g., Jansen/Hermosa etc.) also show capital intensity for mining has risen.

- Less impact from Simandou: Persistent run rates in China steel output around 1Bntpa suggest more marginal tonnes will remain in the market post Simandou than our 2023 expectations when we set our LT price.

- Ore body depletion remains a challenge: A lack of iron ore project investment outside major hubs could also present as upside risk to prices medium term. Bearish iron ore price sentiment due to peak steel in China and Simandou fears have deterred project investment. This hit non-traditional iron ore supply over the next 5-10yrs as reserves are depleted.
- Indian iron ore exports likely to drop longer term: As India's domestic steel industry grows, we believe net exports from the nation will drop.

China's total crude steel output is down 4% April YTD according to NBS. The headline percentage change is uninspiring. But it is interesting to note the April run rate of 1017Mtpa is above any month from April-Dec 2025. On a YoY basis though, it presents down 3% YoY due to the difficult comp in April 2025 (1047Mt third highest in that year). We retain our 2026 forecast for 1Bt, which includes ~60Mt of unreported output. There is upside risk to our forecast given 1Q26 production is already annualising around 1Bt using NBS data. We expect China domestic steel demand to contract 1.5% in 2026 (unchanged from our prior update).

China's iron ore imports rose 30Mt YTD through April – most of this went to port inventory which rose 29Mt over the same period. China steel demand was down ~3.5% YTD in April. The combination of good ore availability and weaker YoY demand isn't translating to lower iron ore prices. This reinforces our thesis that some steel output isn't captured in official statistics (see our deep dive on 2025 steel output vs raw material consumption). It also shows the impact of higher marginal mining costs (cost push).

Iron ore price is up – but so are costs

However, it is interesting to note that based on the move in iron ore prices, margins for first quartile cost Australian producers have potentially risen.

Bulk carrier shipping rates have risen sharply since the start of the conflict in late February. Miners paying to ship from longer distances in Brazil and Africa have been hit harder than those in Australia.
Figure 2: Freight rates vs Oil price

AUD has risen materially since FY26 cost guidance was set, adding further pressure to WA producers in the Pilbara (RIO/BHP/FMG/MIN). FY26 guidance for these has been set at AUD of 65-67c, with FY27 cost guidance likely needing another 5c.
Explosives costs on the rise as well
Explosives comprise 2-5% of the mining costs for iron ore miners. Due to the conflict, ammonium nitrate prices have increased substantially, which will drive mining costs higher as well.
Iron ore inventories – close to record highs but starting to decrease

China iron ore port inventories are at \(\sim 160\mathrm{Mt}\), close to record levels and quite elevated even on a seasonal basis. There are early signs of inventory decline – probably post positive CMRG/BHP negotiation outcomes resulting in draw of BHP built inventories. We continue to point to a lack of correlation between the iron ore price and port inventories – despite the significant market attention on this data series.
